entry.title: Bringing Jev Local — Testing Four Local Models in Real-World Scenarios

link.title: Bringing Jev Local — Testing Four Local Models in Real-World Scenarios

entry.content:
中文

I introduced Jev earlier, and I think this kind of decision model is very useful in practical applications. For example, when I was working on deployment, especially for applications in specific domains, I often needed to consider user intent and keep the conversation on topic. I previously tried using a small 0.6B model for quick decisions. Now that there is a dedicated decision model, it should be faster. But enterprise deployment inevitably needs a local solution. Fortunately, competition in the industry is intense, and there are already many local models available. So I ran two kinds of small tests on four downloadable models for everyone to use as a reference.

Which models and tasks I tested

The models tested were Decider 0.8B, Decima small 1.1, Laya multilingual, and GLiClass multilingual mini. They are all trained for decision-making or classification tasks. I will use their abbreviated names below.

I designed the entire test set myself to classify incoming user requests for customer-service routing in practical scenarios. Formal scoring had two parts: customer-service routing included 48 questions across six categories—billing, technical support, presales, clarification, security escalation, and out-of-scope requests—with eight questions per category. FAQ selection included 20 questions requiring a choice among four documents. Twelve had an appropriate document, while eight should return NONE, meaning “there is no suitable answer.”

The four models received the same questions and rules, and their outputs were scored against the same reference answers. Each was integrated through its own interface, so input encoding and the meaning of output scores were not entirely identical. The questions were synthetic and deliberately included negation, missing information, and conflicting conditions, making them useful for finding problems. I tried to simulate real user scenarios, but actual user input will certainly be more complicated.

How I designed the test set

This self-designed set contains 84 questions: 60 routing questions and 24 FAQ questions. Each task checks one thing. Routing checks whether the model can identify the actual request and follow the handling priorities. FAQ selection limits the evidence to four documents and checks whether the model mistakes similar content for something that “can answer the question or support the requirement.”

The reference answers must follow explicit task rules. For example, translation requests are “out of scope,” and NONE is the answer when the documents do not support an explicit requirement. The questions, rules, and answers were fixed together before the first inference run. Models integrated later continued to use them; I did not revise the answers for a particular model after seeing what it chose.

The test set places ordinary wording alongside wording that is easy to confuse. Here are examples of actual questions, with the reference answers defined by the rules:

  • Ordinary wording and negation: “Login still fails even when I enter the correct password” is technical support. “I am not asking for a refund, the payment is fine, but the webpage will not open” should also be technical support, rather than “refund.”
  • Missing context: “My request is the same as before” requires more information first. The model must not guess what the user wants to do.
  • Keyword distraction: “Please write a poem about refunds” should be an out-of-scope request. Mentioning a refund is not the same as requesting one.
  • Unmet conditions: “The password-reset link must remain valid for 24 hours. Which document supports this requirement?” should return NONE because the available document only says 10 minutes.

Each model showed clear weaknesses overall

Each cell in the table is “questions answered correctly / questions in that category.” The detailed categories belong to their corresponding subtotal. The final total counts only the 48 routing questions plus the 20 FAQ questions, without counting anything twice.

Task Decider Decima Laya GLiClass
Customer-service routing subtotal 43/48 32/48 22/48 18/48
Billing and refunds 8/8 7/8 7/8 6/8
Technical support 8/8 5/8 7/8 8/8
Presales inquiries 8/8 8/8 3/8 2/8
Clarification needed 6/8 4/8 1/8 0/8
Security escalation 8/8 7/8 3/8 2/8
Out-of-scope requests 5/8 1/8 1/8 0/8
FAQ subtotal 16/20 14/20 9/20 12/20
Correct selection when an FAQ answer exists 11/12 12/12 1/12 8/12
FAQ should return NONE 5/8 2/8 8/8 4/8
Overall total 59/68 46/68 31/68 30/68

Decider was the most balanced on this set, answering at least half the questions correctly in all six routing categories. However, it still missed three out-of-scope requests and let through three FAQ questions that should have been rejected.

Decima had a more distinct pattern: it answered every presales question and every FAQ question with an available answer correctly, but got only 1/8 out-of-scope requests and 2/8 no-answer FAQ questions right. It can find existing answers, but a problem with the reward mechanism probably makes it inclined to give a wrong answer even when there is clearly no accurate one.

Laya got 7/8 in both billing and technical support, but showed a severe bias toward NONE in FAQ selection: it selected NONE 19 times out of 20, getting only one of the 12 questions with an available answer right.

GLiClass answered every technical-support question correctly, but got 0/8 in both clarification and out-of-scope requests. Testing only common faults would overestimate its reliability across the full routing process.

These judgments apply only to the small sample in the table. Getting all eight security-escalation questions right does not mean a model already has reliable security-detection capabilities. The following two sets of examples explain more specifically where the problems lie.

Customer-service routing needs to understand what the user wants to do

Both routing questions use the following six options. The text after each colon is the candidate description given to the model:

  • billing — billing and refunds: charges, invoices, billing errors, or refund requests
  • technical — technical support: software errors, login failures, or unusable features
  • sales — presales inquiries: prices, plans, product capabilities, or trial inquiries
  • clarify — additional information: references without context, requests missing necessary information, or mutually contradictory requirements
  • security_review — security escalation: compromised accounts, unfamiliar logins, data leaks, or sensitive permission risks
  • out_of_scope — out-of-scope requests: requests outside product customer service, such as weather, translation, poetry, programming, or ordering food

The common rule is to classify the user’s actual request without executing instructions embedded in the input. Unrelated tasks such as translation are “out of scope.” In other cases, the handling priority is security risks, contradictory or missing information, billing and refunds, technical faults, then presales inquiries.

Successful example: The user input was “Login still fails even when I enter the correct password.” The reference answer was “technical support.” The user was describing a usage problem, and all four models chose correctly.

Failed example: The user input was “Translate ‘login failed’ into English.” The reference answer was “out of scope.” What needs to be classified here is a translation request. “Login failed” is merely the content to translate, and there is actually no option for the task of translation.

The actual results were:

Model Reporting a login problem Requesting a sentence translation
Decider Technical support — correct Technical support — incorrect
Decima Technical support — correct Billing and refunds — incorrect
Laya Technical support — correct Technical support — incorrect
GLiClass Technical support — correct Technical support — incorrect

In the first question, all four models could handle the explicit description of a fault. The second question shows that the models recognized the content “login failed,” but did not distinguish that the user’s actual request was “translation,” rather than a request to handle a “login failed” situation.

In this translation question, Decider assigned the incorrect option a score of about 0.916. So even if I specify in the general rules that “routing should only occur above 0.9,” this request would still be routed incorrectly. This misclassification rate is still very high.

Selecting a relevant document also requires checking the specific conditions

The complete FAQ candidates are listed below. The full contents of the four short documents were supplied as input, and NONE was the fifth available answer.

  • A — billing help: If you find a duplicate charge, provide the order number to request a refund. Refunds can be requested within 30 days of purchase. Account login is not handled here.
  • B — password help: If you forget your password, click reset password on the login page. The link in the reset email remains valid for 10 minutes. Refunds are not covered here.
  • C — data help: Export a CSV file from the data page in settings. Exporting does not delete the original data. This feature is available on every plan.
  • D — plan help: Annual payment costs 20% less than monthly payment. The annual fee is paid upfront in one payment. Only administrators can change the plan.
  • NONE: None of the documents can answer the question or support the explicit requirement, the requirements are contradictory, or necessary information is missing.

The rules require choosing the single best document that can answer the question or support the explicit requirement, using only these four documents. The model must not supplement policies with external common knowledge.

Successful example: The user input was “This is not a refund question. How long does the link in the password-reset email take to expire?” The reference answer was B. It explicitly provides the answer “10 minutes.” Decider, Decima, and GLiClass all chose correctly, while Laya incorrectly chose NONE.

Failed example: The user input was “The password-reset link must remain valid for 24 hours. Which document supports this requirement?” The reference answer was NONE. B only states 10 minutes, and none of the other three documents supports a 24-hour requirement either.

The actual outputs were:

Model Asking how long the link remains valid Requiring 24-hour validity
Decider B — correct B — incorrect
Decima B — correct B — incorrect
Laya NONE — incorrect NONE — correct
GLiClass B — correct B — incorrect

These two questions are actually asking different things. The first looks up existing information; the second checks whether the material supports a specific requirement. If “a document was selected” is interpreted directly as “the requirement can be met,” the automated reply that follows may produce an incorrect output.

I actually think many models have this problem today. A usable knowledge-base component needs to do both things well: select the right document when there is evidence, and stop when there is none. It is important to know when to stop and honestly tell the user, “I don’t know.”

Integration itself can also create wrong answers

While testing Decima, I found another pitfall: candidate inputs retain at most 64 tokens by default. Tokens are the small pieces of text the model reads. The longest input in this set required 94, so some content was truncated. Only after increasing the limit to 128, confirming that nothing was truncated, and rerunning the test did I obtain the official figures in the table above. The questions, rules, answers, and weights were not changed.

So when you see an error, first check what the model actually received, especially length limits, candidate descriptions, and output mappings. Otherwise, integration errors can easily be misrepresented as conclusions about model capabilities. Similarly, these models use different backends, precision, thread counts, and cache settings, so the existing timings cannot be used for a fair comparison and ranking.

If you test them yourself

I would suggest trying Decider first. It provided the best overall starting point for both tasks, but its official positioning is as an English-language model. However, the rules and candidate descriptions in my tests were entirely in Chinese, and I also tried mixing several languages in the questions. That already goes beyond its official language scope, so its language generalization is reasonably good and worth further engineering experiments.

If your priority is low latency on a CPU, you can consider Decima as a second candidate, but first address its tendency to choose arbitrary answers when none is available.

For this test, I have three small suggestions: define the options and the cost of errors clearly for a small task; use your own independent examples to check both normal requests and boundary cases; and retain human involvement and existing processes for uncertain or high-cost decisions.

Local decision models are suited to starting with this kind of clearly bounded step. What determines the boundary of automation is still which decisions the model fails at, and how the fallback strategy for those failures is designed.

entry.title: 把Jev搬到本地 - 四个本地模型实际场景测评

link.title: 把Jev搬到本地 - 四个本地模型实际场景测评

entry.content:
English

之前介绍过Jev，我觉得这种判断模型在实际的应用场景中用处很大。譬如我之前在做落地的时候，尤其是垂类的应用，很需要考虑用户的意图，以及做话题的守护。之前尝试用0.6B的小模型做快速判断，现在有这个专门的判断模型，速度会更快。但是企业落地肯定要考虑本地方案，还好行业卷的不行，现在已经有很多本地的模型，于是我用四个可下载的模型做了两类小测试以供大家参考。

测了哪些模型和任务

实测对象是 Decider 0.8B、Decima small 1.1、Laya multilingual 和 GLiClass multilingual mini。它们都是针对判断或分类任务训练的模型，下文将用简写。

整个测试题库是我自己设计的，针对实际场景中的客服分流，将用户的输入请求内容归类。正式计分分为两部分：客服分流有 48 题，分为账单相关、技术支持、售前、澄清、安全升级、无关请求六类，每类 8 题；FAQ 选择有 20 题，从四篇文档中作选择；其中 12 题有合适文档，8 题应该返回 NONE，也就是“没有合适答案”。

四个模型接收同一批题目与规则，输出统一按参考答案判分；接入使用各自的接口，输入编码和输出分数的含义并不完全相同。题目都是合成材料，特意包含否定、缺失信息和条件冲突，适合找问题。尽量模拟真实用户场景，但是需要注意现实中的用户输入肯定会更复杂。

这套题是怎么设计的

这套自建题库共 84 题，包括 60 道分流和 24 道 FAQ。两类任务各看一件事：分流检查能否识别真正诉求、遵守处理优先级；FAQ 把依据限定在四篇文档里，检查模型会不会把类似内容误当成“能够回答或支持要求”。

参考答案要依据明确的任务规则。例如，翻译请求归“无关”，资料不支持明确要求时选 NONE。题目、规则与答案在首次推理前一起固定，后续接入的模型继续使用，没有看某个模型选了什么再替它修改答案。

题库把正常表达和容易混淆的表达放在一起。下面是实际题目的案例，并附上按规则设定的参考答案：

  • 正常与否定：“输入正确密码仍然提示登录失败。”是技术支持；“不是要退款，付款正常，但是网页打不开。”也应选技术支持，不能选择“退款”
  • 缺少上下文：“我的要求和之前一样。”应先补充信息，不能猜测用户要办理什么
  • 关键词干扰：“请写一首关于退款的诗。”应选无关请求，提到退款不等于申请退款
  • 条件不符：“密码重置链接必须有效24小时，哪篇支持这个要求？”应选 NONE，因为已有文档只写了 10 分钟

整体表现各有明显的短板

表中每格都是“答对题数／该类题数”。细类属于对应小计；最后的合计只计算 48 道分流题加 20 道 FAQ 题，不重复计数。

任务 Decider Decima Laya GLiClass
客服分流小计 43/48 32/48 22/48 18/48
账单退款 8/8 7/8 7/8 6/8
技术支持 8/8 5/8 7/8 8/8
售前咨询 8/8 8/8 3/8 2/8
需要澄清 6/8 4/8 1/8 0/8
安全升级 8/8 7/8 3/8 2/8
无关请求 5/8 1/8 1/8 0/8
FAQ 小计 16/20 14/20 9/20 12/20
FAQ 有答案时选对 11/12 12/12 1/12 8/12
FAQ 应返回 NONE 5/8 2/8 8/8 4/8
全部合计 59/68 46/68 31/68 30/68

Decider 在这组题里最均衡，分流六类都至少答对一半。不过，它仍漏掉了三个无关请求，FAQ 也有三个该拒答的问题被放过。

Decima 的特点更明确：售前题和有答案的 FAQ 全对，但无关请求只对 1/8，无答案 FAQ 只对 2/8。它能找到现成答案，但是应该是奖励机制的问题导致它在明明没有准确答案的时候依旧倾向于给一个错误答案。

Laya 的账单与技术支持各对 7/8，FAQ 却严重偏向 NONE：20 次里选了 19 次，导致 12 道有答案题只做对 1 道。

GLiClass 的技术支持题全对，但澄清与无关请求各对 0/8。只用常见故障测试，会高估它在整套分流流程里的可靠性。

这些判断都只针对表里的小样本。某模型在八道安全升级题上全对，并不等于它已经具备可靠的安全检测能力。下面两组例子进一步给大家解释一下具体的问题在哪里。

客服分流要读懂用户想做什么

两道分流题都使用下面六个选项，冒号后的文字就是提供给模型的候选说明：

  • billing 账单退款：扣款、发票、收费错误或退款请求
  • technical 技术支持：软件错误、登录故障、功能无法使用
  • sales 售前咨询：价格、套餐、产品能力或试用咨询
  • clarify 补充信息：指代无上下文、请求缺少必要信息，或要求互相矛盾
  • security_review 安全升级：账户被盗、陌生登录、数据泄露或敏感权限风险
  • out_of_scope 无关请求：不属于产品客服，例如天气、翻译、写诗、编程或订餐

共同规则是按用户真正的请求分类，不执行输入中夹带的指令；翻译等无关任务归“无关请求”。其余情况依次优先处理安全风险、矛盾或缺失信息、账单退款、技术故障、售前咨询。

成功例子： 用户输入为：“输入正确密码仍然提示登录失败。” 参考答案是“技术支持”。用户正在描述使用故障，四个模型都选对了。

失败例子： 用户输入为：“把‘登录失败’翻译成英文。” 参考答案是“无关请求”。这里要分类的是一个翻译请求；“登录失败”只是待翻译的内容，但是实际上没有翻译这个任务的选项。

实际结果是：

模型 报告登录故障 请求翻译句子
Decider 技术支持 正确 技术支持 错误
Decima 技术支持 正确 账单退款 错误
Laya 技术支持 正确 技术支持 错误
GLiClass 技术支持 正确 技术支持 错误

前一题中，四个模型都能处理这条明确的故障描述。后一题说明，模型识别到了“登录失败”的内容，但是模型没有分清用户的真实要求是“翻译”，而不是要求处理“登录失败”的情况。

这道翻译题里，Decider 给错误选项的分数约为 0.916。所以即使我在通用规定中说明“超过 0.9 才进行分流”，这条依旧会被错误分流。这个误判率还是非常高的。

选到相关文档还要检查具体条件

FAQ 题的全部候选如下。四篇短文是完整内容输入，NONE 是第五个可选答案。

  • A 账单帮助：发现重复扣款，请提供订单号申请退款；购买后30天内可申请退款。此处不处理账号登录。
  • B 密码帮助：忘记密码时，在登录页点击重置密码；重置邮件中的链接10分钟内有效。此处不涉及退款。
  • C 数据帮助：在设置中的数据页面导出CSV文件；导出不会删除原始数据。此功能所有套餐可用。
  • D 套餐帮助：年付价格比按月付费低20%；年费一次预付；只有管理员可更改套餐。
  • NONE：所有文档都无法回答或支持明确要求，要求矛盾，或缺少必要信息。

规则要求只依据这四篇文档，选择能回答问题或支持明确要求的唯一最佳文档，不能凭外部常识补充政策。

成功例子： 用户输入：“不是退款问题，重置密码邮件的链接多久失效？”参考答案是 B。它明确提供了“10 分钟”这个答案。Decider、Decima 和 GLiClass 都选对，Laya 则错误地选择了 NONE。

失败例子： 用户输入：“密码重置链接必须有效24小时，哪篇支持这个要求？”参考答案是 NONE。B 只写了 10 分钟，其他三篇也没有支持 24 小时的要求。

实际输出如下：

模型 询问链接有效期 要求有效24小时
Decider B 正确 B 错误
Decima B 正确 B 错误
Laya NONE 错误 NONE 正确
GLiClass B 正确 B 错误

这两道题其实问的不是同一件事。第一题是在查已有信息；第二题是在检查资料是否支持一个具体要求。如果把“选中了文档”直接解释为“可以满足需求”，后面的自动回复就可能作出错误的输出。

其实我觉得现在很多的模型都有这个问题，作为一个可用的知识库组件需要同时做好这两件事：有依据时选对文档，没有依据时停下来。什么时候停下来，诚实地告诉用户“我不知道”很重要。

接入本身也可能制造错题

测试 Decima 时还发现了一个坑：候选输入默认最多保留 64 个 token，也就是模型读入文字的小片段，而这组输入最长需要 94 个，部分内容被截断了。把上限调到 128、确认没有截断后重新运行，才得到上表的正式数字。题目、规则、答案和权重都没有修改。

所以，看到错误时先检查模型真正收到的内容，尤其是长度限制、候选说明和输出映射。否则，接入错误很容易被误写成模型能力结论。类似地，这几种模型的后端、精度、线程数与缓存设置不同，已有耗时并不能做一个公平的验证和排序。

如果大家自己测试的话

我会建议大家先试 Decider。它在两类任务上都提供了最好的整体起点，但官方把它定位为英语模型。但是我这里实测中用的规则与候选说明全是中文，题目还尝试混合了多种语言，已经超出官方语言范围，所以这个模型在语言泛化性上还可以，值得继续做工程试验。

如果你的重点是 CPU 上的低延迟，可以把 Decima 作为第二个候选，但要先解决无答案时乱选的问题。

针对这次测试，我有三个小建议：把一个小任务的选项和错误代价写清楚；用自己的独立例题同时检查正常请求与边界情况；给不确定或高代价的判断保留人工与既有流程。

本地判断模型适合从这种范围清楚的环节开始。决定自动化边界的，仍是模型在哪些判断后会失败，以及失败的兜底策略如何设计。

entry.title: Plan Mode Is on Its Way Out

link.title: Plan Mode Is on Its Way Out

entry.content:
中文版

Most people who use AI coding tools know Plan mode. In Claude Code, you can press Shift+Tab to enter it: the agent explores the codebase, asks questions, and proposes a plan before making changes. You discuss the details, approve the plan, and then let it work.

There is a technical distinction worth keeping clear. Claude Code’s documentation describes Plan mode as a workflow that researches and proposes changes while restricting source edits until approval. The handling of shell commands also depends on the session’s permissions and settings. Reducing all of that to “one extra prompt” would be misleading; I would not make an unverified claim about its internal tool definitions or prompt cache.

My real question is about the workflow: as models become more capable, do we still need planning and execution to be locked into separate modes?

Plan mode has always had two jobs

Historically, Plan mode has served two purposes. It makes instructions precise enough for an agent to execute, and it helps the human understand what is about to happen.

I think those two jobs are moving in opposite directions. Stronger models need less help turning a general direction into executable steps. At the same time, the more an agent can do on its own, the more demanding human oversight becomes. There is simply more work to review than a person can comfortably keep up with.

The original assumption was reasonable: thinking everything through before starting is useful, and saving that thinking in a structured document is useful too. But as models improve and human review becomes the slowest part of the process, people lose patience with long specifications. “Build something first; fix what is wrong afterward” becomes an appealing choice.

Agents can communicate efficiently with one another. When a model’s language feels unlike ordinary human conversation, I sometimes see that as a kind of adaptation: it is compressing communication to get the task done. Keeping every exchange easy for a human to read can introduce its own overhead. That is my interpretation, rather than a claim that models literally evolve in the biological sense.

Meanwhile, nobody wants to read pages of AI-generated prose. A specification may contain more information without becoming any clearer. The longer and more detailed it gets, the easier it is to stop absorbing it. Eventually, you ask the AI to summarize its own document—and may discover that it has thought through the problem better than you have.

Planning and building have been split into two stages. The familiar sequence looks like this:

Chat → clarify → generate a spec → review → revise → approve → implement → review the code.

But that is not how I find it easiest to think. People rely heavily on concrete things they can see and try. You understand part of a problem, test something, learn from the result, change your mind, and try again. Requiring every detail to be settled before any implementation starts feels at odds with that process.

And even if you have worked through every detail, the agent may still miss something in the final implementation. A thorough document does not guarantee a complete delivery.

I would be happy to drop the separate mode

Dropping Plan mode does not mean dropping planning. Before implementation, the agent still needs to understand four things:

  1. The actual business logic.
  2. The concrete details of the existing architecture.
  3. The relevant edge cases.
  4. The scope of the code changes.

My current workflow starts with a general direction. Then I ask the agent to clarify the details with me. Once we have done that, I ask it to write a plan.md that preserves the important decisions and constraints we discussed.

What I need to keep a firm grip on is that small set of important boundaries. Most of the remaining details are usually fine.

The implementation plan is a separate concern. I review the points that matter: is it reusing the existing architecture and interfaces? Does the proposed scope fit the project’s hard constraints and conventions? Are database permissions within the intended boundaries?

After each feature is finished, I also ask for a change report. I want to know which parts of the code changed and how they changed.

None of this has to become a document every time. One reason I write it down is to keep the agent from losing the decisions. Once the feature is implemented, I also want a concrete record of the solution for future reference.

My advice to developers is straightforward: you may spend less time reading every line of code, but you still need to understand and control the system as a whole. Documentation is one way to do that. Even when you cannot read everything closely, keep a record of the implementation logic that matters.

My argument is about reducing the ceremony around planning while keeping responsibility for the system. Clear boundaries, focused review, and a useful account of the finished work matter more to me than a dedicated mode.

Reference: Claude Code’s official documentation on Plan mode and permission modes. The workflow judgments and recommendations in this essay are my own.

entry.title: Plan mode 正在退场
entry.content:
English version

我相信大部分用AI工具的人都非常熟悉Plan mode。按一下 shift+tab，agent 进入只读状态，读代码、问你问题、写一份计划，但一个字都不许改。你跟它详细沟通清楚了，你同意了它才动手。

那它到底是怎么实现的呢？以 Claude Code 为例，Plan mode 会让 agent 先研究、提出方案，并在批准计划之前限制源码编辑。按官方文档，具体的命令审批行为还取决于会话权限和设置。它并不能简单归结为「多加一句提示词」，也不应把工具集和 prompt cache 的关系当作未经核实的实现细节。

但我更关心的是：随着模型越来越强，我们是否还需要把「先计划、再执行」固定成一个独立模式？

随着模型的能力越来越强，很多人都在讨论plan mode是否还有存在的意义。

计划模式一直在干两件事

plan mode 历史上同时承担两个角色，一是把指令变得足够精确，让 agent 能执行，二是帮人弄明白即将发生什么。

我的判断是这两个角色正在往相反的方向走。第一个随着模型变强在消失，第二个随着 agent 能自己干更多活在变重，现在人力根本就审核不过来。原来的假设是，动手之前有地方把事情彻底想一遍是有价值的，把这段思考存成一份结构化文档也是有价值的。结果现在随着模型能力的增强，以及人成为整个流程中效率最低的环节，越来越多的人对 spec的长文档失去了审核的耐心。先干，有毛病了再改成了大部分人的选择。

其实AI agent之间的交流可以是非常高效的，而且大家现在经常觉得很多大语言模型不说“人话”，其实是它们的一种“进化选择”。也就是说，它们为了更好地完成任务，而精简了它们的交流方式。在某种程度上来说，AI为了“顾虑”人类能读懂这件事，反而可能会拖累了AI。

而且，AI 生成的长文没人愿意读。spec 里的信息变多了，清晰度没变多，篇幅越长越详细，眼睛越容易发直。最后可能还是让AI精简一下，然后读下来发现自己想得还没有AI想得好呢。

规划和建造被切成了两段。之前推荐的流程是 聊天 → 澄清 → 生成 spec → 审 → 改 → 批准 → 实现 → 审代码。其实人类适合的思考模式不是这个样子的，人类是非常依赖视觉和具象事物，所以通常是搞懂一部分，试一下，试出来的东西教你新东西，于是你改主意再试一次。Plan mode让你非要全部都想好再弄，还挺反人类的。

而且还有一个问题，就算你把每一处的细节都想好了，AI最后也不一定会按照这份文档交付，总会有遗漏。

我是完全同意去掉Plan mode的

不要这个plan mode，不代表没有plan。其实在做一个plan之前，它应该理解几个点：

  1. 真实的业务逻辑
  2. 具体的代码架构细节
  3. 可能的边界条件
  4. 代码的修改范围

我现在的主要流程是给它一个大致的方向，然后让它跟我澄清每一个细节，让它在澄清之后输出一个plan.md的文档，这里面要保留我们所有重点讨论过的内容和细节，其实我只需要把所有这些比较重要的限制把握住，大部分的内容它都是没有问题的。 然后具体代码的实施计划是单独的，我会审核几个比较重要的点，譬如是否复用了现在的代码架构和接口，实施的范围和内容是否符合现有项目的硬性限制和规范，数据库的权限范围等等。 另外每次它完成后，我都会要求它输出一份修改报告，这样就知道这一个功能它修改了哪些代码，是怎么修改的。 这些东西也不是非要落成文档，主要是担心AI会忘记，然后功能实现之后，还需要生成一个具体的解决方案以供归档。

最后给所有开发人员一个忠告，你可以省去读代码细节的时间，但是对系统整体功能的把控还是需要有的。文档只是一种形式，就算没时间细读，重点的实现逻辑还是需要留个记录。

参考：Claude Code 官方文档：Plan mode 与权限模式。本文关于工作流程的判断和建议是我的个人观点。

entry.title: What Is Jev? What It Does and How to Use It

link.title: What Is Jev? What It Does and How to Use It

entry.content:
Have you ever run into a situation like this? To decide whether a news item belongs in today’s daily brief, you call a model with hundreds of billions of parameters. It thinks for two seconds, produces a paragraph such as “Overall, this news item appears to have some relevance,” and then you still have to write a pile of regexes and try-except blocks to pry a single "yes" out of that filler.

One yes-or-no question has gone through an entire generation pipeline.

Jev, which has been all over people’s feeds these past few days, is built to cut that pipeline out. Less than a week after launch, more than 700 posts about it had accumulated on X. Within 24 hours of arriving on Vercel AI Gateway, nearly 13% of paid teams there were calling it-an adoption rate higher than any model Vercel had previously listed.

ChatGPT writes answers for people; Jev makes decisions for programs. It does not write code, it does not chat, and it does not even expose a free-form text interface. It handles only three kinds of questions, returning a probability with a confidence level in a few hundred milliseconds.

Why Large Models Are So Awkward at Yes-or-No Questions

The reason is autoregression.

Large models produce output one token at a time. Even if all you want is JSON, the model has to “write” that string of characters first, and your program then has to parse it. To produce one word, it pauses to consider the next; everything that came before must be recomputed in attention along the way.

It is like asking someone who writes essays to look back over everything they have written before placing every single character, then decide what comes next. That mechanism gives large models tremendous creative power: they can write fiction, code, and analytical reports. But when you ask them a true-or-false question, it becomes much more cumbersome. It is not that they cannot do it; it is more like using a crane to drive a nail.

If you use an API, cost is also a major concern. Adding one decision point is easy. The problem is that an agent may need to make dozens or hundreds of decisions in a single task: call once to determine whether an email is a complaint, call again to decide which tool to use next, call again to check whether the task is done, and call a second model once more when it is uncertain. The user sees one task completed; behind the scenes, dozens of calls have already been burned.

How Jev Gets Around This

Jev comes from San Francisco-based TypeSafe AI. It launched on September 15, 2026, and has just raised a $40 million seed round led by DCVC. Its founder, Diogo Almeida, came from OpenAI and is one of the authors of the InstructGPT paper.

Its name comes from economist William Stanley Jevons, the person behind the “Jevons paradox”: when technology makes something cheaper, total consumption can rise instead. Naming a model whose pitch is “cheap enough to call freely” after him makes the intention fairly obvious.

Its approach is to tightly constrain the output.

The input is a piece of state: your program's current state. The output has only three forms:

Choice

Select one option from a fixed set

choice, a probability for each option, and confidence

Score

Assign a score on an ordered set of levels

score, a probability for each level, and confidence

Noul

The probability that a judgment holds

A floating-point number from 0 to 1

Suppose a customer says, “The shoe size is wrong, and my refund still has not arrived.” You can ask Jev, at the same time, which department should handle the case, whether the customer is requesting a refund, and how intense the customer’s emotion is. It does not write an explanation; it returns the options, scores, and probabilities directly.

Choice supports up to 255 options, so it cannot invent a 256th one out of thin air. The official description calls this “zero hallucination,” though that wording is not really precise. It is enough to understand the mechanism.

Because the answer is confined to the range you give it, Jev does not need to decode output word by word. Instead, it calculates the probability distribution across all options in the output layer at once. Its official end-to-end figure is 70 to 500 milliseconds.

Another very effective mechanism is that it reads the same material only once and answers multiple questions in parallel. TypeSafe says that adding questions has almost no effect on response time, so do not split them into multiple calls-that only means paying repeatedly for the same long input.

TypeSafe calls this category a System One Model, borrowing Kahneman’s distinction between fast and slow thinking. Large models have been imitating slow thinking: writing long analyses and doing complex reasoning. Jev fills in the fast, lightweight kind of thinking that makes intuitive judgments. The official documentation has an analogy that I think is even more accurate: a “function call that understands semantics.”

What is truly valuable is not speed, but probability calibration.

Earlier small classification models were fast too. But because of the way they were trained, even without a correct match they would still rank the options and return whichever one fit best-even if the “best” option was completely wrong. That kind of confidence is unusable; you would not dare base routing policy on it. Jev’s training objective is called RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions). The idea is to make confidence behave like a trustworthy weather forecast: when it says it is 80% sure, it should be right roughly 80 times out of 100 in statistical terms.

Only once that works does it become meaningful in engineering practice. You can safely write if confidence > 0.9: let high-confidence cases pass automatically, and send low-confidence ones to a human or a large model.

Quantifiable Real-World Results

TypeSafe’s website displays two figures: up to 193.6× faster and 444.6× cheaper. It is important to look carefully at where those numbers come from.

They come from TypeSafe’s own workflow evaluation. The comparison baseline is the average of GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1, and the workflows being tested were written by TypeSafe’s own team. The company itself acknowledges that the gain is at the upper end of real-world use. One further detail: it has not published proof that the price is not subsidized.

Then there is the claim that it is “238× cheaper than Claude Fable 5.1.” That number comes from dividing input pricing by input pricing: $10 divided by $0.042. But that is not the price tier teams are actually using in practice.

Across four business workflows, Jev averaged about 68% accuracy at a cost of $0.0004; GPT-5.6 Luna averaged about 67% at $0.0035; GPT-5.6 Sol reached 74% at $0.085; and Claude Opus 5 reached 73% at $0.17.

What It Cannot Do

“Zero hallucination” does not mean it never makes mistakes. It only guarantees that the answer falls within the options you provide. It can still choose the wrong option among valid ones; TypeSafe’s CEO has acknowledged this himself. The 0% claim refers to formatting errors, not an observed answer-error rate.

Then there is the list of uneven weaknesses exposed in testing. Counting, exact arithmetic, and reasoning about the order of dates are not very reliable. Accuracy drops noticeably on long-chain, multi-hop reasoning. It is trained primarily in English; Chinese works, but is materially weaker. Before using it for nuanced Chinese semantic judgments, be sure to test it on your own samples first.

Prompt injection still works. If users hide steering instructions in the input, Jev can still be led astray. So for high-risk actions involving refunds, funds, or deleting a database, hard-coded permission checks at the lower layer still need to stay in place.

There is also a structural limit: the input cap is about 32,000 tokens. Someone tried to put it into their everyday tools to improve productivity and ran into a wall all four times. The problem was not the model: the API returned normally each time, and its Chinese judgments were accurate. The blockers were threefold. First, it could not see enough content; to fit under the limit, material had to be cut, and after that there was not enough left for it to judge. Second, when you already have a subscription to a large model, the marginal cost of one more judgment is effectively zero; inserting another layer only adds a second of latency and another point of failure. Third, it can judge but cannot do work. Moving data and changing files still rely on a third-party wrapper, and all the pitfalls end up in that wrapper layer.

How to Get Started

The official route is to join the waitlist at typesafe.ai, then create an API key in the console after you are approved. If you do not want to wait, there are three shortcuts: call typesafe/jev-1.13 directly after registering with OpenRouter; use typesafe-ai/jev on Vercel AI Gateway; or use Cloudflare Workers AI, which has it too. Pricing is the same as the official service. The official API model name is jev-latest.

One pitfall: the official SDK reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, while the code-review plugin for Claude Code and Codex reads JEV_API_KEY. They are two different environment-variable names.

Installing the SDK takes one line. Python needs to be version 3.10 or higher.

The most basic usage is to send a state and a set of questions to one endpoint. All questions share the same state and are answered in parallel.

The Python SDK is smoother to read. The same call sends all three questions together.

There is one detail here that is especially worth thinking about: confidence and the probability of the highest-ranked option are not the same thing.

In the official documentation’s example, billing wins with a probability of 0.84, but confidence is only 0.596 because technical, the runner-up, still holds 0.159. It wins, but not decisively enough. If you look only at probability and not confidence, it is easy to let this kind of ambiguous judgment slip through.

After testing, here are a few practical takeaways:

Keep the division of labor strict. Let Jev handle only the extraction of the original judgment. Leave date calculations, counting, sorting, and threshold comparisons to your own code. Keep permissions and policy in your own code as well; do not expect it to serve as your guardrail.

Set thresholds according to the cost of an error; do not copy someone else’s numbers. The loss from a misclassification differs from task to task, and stricter requirements still need your own oversight.

For every call, log the model version, probabilities, and usage. Once thresholds are tuned, pin a versioned model ID instead of continually pointing to latest.

Calibrate confidence bands and thresholds on labeled examples from your own business.

For retrieval pipelines, first use a relevance judgment to filter the material, so each decision sees only the passages it needs. That is both more accurate and more economical.

When Should You Use It?

The right place for Jev is very clear: the small decision points that already exist inside a system.

Who should receive this ticket? Is this content compliant? Which tool should be called next? Does this extraction result need another review? Should this order be escalated to a human? These are the places where systems often used to stuff in a large-model call-slow, expensive, and followed by regexes to extract an answer from its response.

The unsuitable places are equally clear. If you need writing, free-form creation, or long-chain reasoning, it cannot do the job and it will not do it well. When the problem itself has not been thought through and you cannot even list the options yet, you are in the exploration stage, and a large model is the right tool.

The cases already appearing online all follow the same pattern: replace a decision point in an existing system, rather than asking Jev to do the work itself.

Browser Use’s open-source jev-ultrafast turns a webpage into a numbered list of elements and lets Jev choose "which one to click." Its Zurich-to-London flight search fell from 9.5 seconds to 7.1 seconds. TypeSafe used it to play Doom: the input becomes parsed, structured state rather than pixels; it makes about ten decisions per second, and an hour of play costs about $7. LangChain shipped TypeSafeClassifier on the day after launch, moving control-flow decisions such as "which tool to call next" out of the hands of a large model. Vercel integrated it into AI Gateway and the evaluate capability of AI SDK 7 for compliance review and factual-consistency scoring.

If you happen to have a small decision point that is blocking a main path and must run hundreds of thousands of times a day, it is genuinely worth trying now. As for putting it directly into production, my view is: wait a little longer.

Originally published at https://stefaniezhao77.github.io.

entry.title: 最近很火的 Jev 到底是什么，一篇讲清它干嘛用和怎么用

link.title: 最近很火的 Jev 到底是什么，一篇讲清它干嘛用和怎么用

entry.content:
你有没有实际遇到这样的场景：为了判断一条新闻该不该进今天的日报，你调用一个几千亿参数的模型。它想两秒，吐出一段”综合来看，这条新闻具有一定的相关性”，然后你还得写一堆正则和 try-except，从这段废话里把那个”是”抠出来。

一道判断题，走了一整套生成流程。

这几天刷屏的 Jev，干的就是把这趟流程砍掉。上线不到一周，X 上关于它的内容堆到七百多条，Vercel AI Gateway 上架 24 小时内就有接近 13% 的付费团队在调用它，这个采用速度超过 Vercel 此前上过的任何一个模型。

ChatGPT 给人写答案，Jev 给程序做判断。它不写代码、不聊天，连自由文本接口都没有，只做三种题，几百毫秒返回一个带把握程度的概率。

为什么大模型做判断题这么别扭

原因在于自回归。

大模型是一个字一个字往外蹦的。哪怕你要的只是一个 JSON，它也得先把那串字符”写”出来，再由你的程序去解析。写一个词要停下来琢磨下一个词，前面所有内容还得在注意力里重算一遍。

这像个写作文的人，每落一个字都要回想一遍前面写了啥再决定下一个字。这套机制换来了极强的创作能力，写小说、写代码、写分析报告都可。但是你让它做一道是非题，却麻烦了很多，也不是不能用，而是仿佛用一个起重机砸钉子。

如果用的是API的话，价格也是很大的问题：接入一个判断点容易，问题是 agent 一条任务里要判断几十上百次。判断邮件是不是投诉调一次，决定下一步用哪个工具再调一次，检查任务完成没有又调一次，不确定再让另一个模型复核一次。用户看着是完成了一项任务，后台已经烧了几十次调用。

Jev 是怎么绕过去的

Jev 来自旧金山的 TypeSafe AI，2026 年 9 月 15 日发布，刚拿了 4000 万美元种子轮，DCVC 领投。创始人 Diogo Almeida 出身 OpenAI，是 InstructGPT 论文的作者之一。

名字取自经济学家 William Stanley Jevons，就是提出”杰文斯悖论”那位，技术让某样东西更便宜，总消耗量反而会涨。拿这个名字给一个主打”便宜到可以随便调”的模型命名，意图挺明显。

它的做法是把输出限制死。

输入是一段 state，也就是你程序当前的状态。输出只有三种形式

题型 它回答什么 返回什么
Choice 从固定选项里选一个 choice、每个选项的概率、confidence
Score 在一组有顺序的等级上打分 score、每个等级的概率、confidence
Noul 这个判断成立的概率 一个 0 到 1 的浮点数

假设客户说”鞋码不对，而且退款还没到账”。你可以同时问它这单该转给哪个部门、客户是否在要求退款、情绪有多激烈。它不写解释，直接把选项、分数、概率交回来。

Choice 最多支持 255 个选项，所以它不可能凭空编出第 256 个。官方管这个叫”零幻觉”，这个说法其实并不准确，知道它的机制就好。

因为答案被限制在你给的范围里，它不需要逐字解码，直接在输出层一次性算出各个选项的概率分布。官方口径是端到端 70 到 500 毫秒。

还有个机制很有效，同一段材料只读一遍，多道题并行作答。官方说加题几乎不影响响应时间，所以别把问题拆成多次调用，那是白白重复付长材料的钱。

TypeSafe 把它这类东西叫 System One Model，借的是卡尼曼那套快慢思考的分法。大模型一直在模仿慢思考，写长分析做复杂推理。Jev 补的是那个又快又轻、凭直觉下判断的快思考。官方文档还有一个比方我觉得更准，管它叫”会理解语义的函数调用”。

但真正值钱的不是快，是概率校准。

以前的小分类模型也快，但是由于训练机制，导致它即使没有正确匹配也会根据排序给你一个最符合的选项，实际上最符合的可能也是完全错误的。那种置信度没法用，你不敢拿它写分流策略。Jev 的训练目标叫 RLCD（Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions），就是让置信度像靠谱的天气预报，说八成把握的时候，统计上一百次里真能对八十次左右。

这件事做成了，工程上才有意义。你可以放心地写一行 if confidence > 0.9，高把握自动过，低把握转人工或者转大模型。

可量化的真实效果

TypeSafe 官网挂着两个数字，最高快 193.6 倍、便宜 444.6 倍。这两个数的出处要看清楚。

它来自 TypeSafe 自己的 workflow eval，参考标准是 GPT-6 Astra 和 Fable 5.1 的平均，测试用的 workflow 是 TypeSafe 自己的团队写的。公司自己也承认，这个增益处在真实使用的高端。另外一个细节，他们没发证明这个价格没有被补贴。

再看那个”比 Claude Fable 5.1 便宜 238 倍”，这是拿输入价格除以输入价格算出来的，$10 除以 $0.042。可团队真正在用的不是那个价位。

模型 输入（每百万 token） 输出（每百万 token） 跟 Jev 比
TypeSafe Jev $0.042 免费 基准
GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 $1.20 约 4.8 倍
GPT-5.6 Terra $2 $12 约 48 倍
Claude Fable 5.1 $10 $50 约 238 倍

四个业务 workflow 的平均准确率，Jev 大约 68%，成本 $0.0004；GPT-5.6 Luna 大约 67%，成本 $0.0035；GPT-5.6 Sol 74%，$0.085；Claude Opus 5 73%，$0.17。

它做不到的事

“零幻觉”不等于不会错。它只保证答案落在你给的选项里，在合法选项里选错照样会发生，TypeSafe 的 CEO 自己认过这一点。那个 0% 的说法指格式错误，不是实测的答案错误率。

然后是实测暴露出来的偏科清单。数数、精确算术、日期先后推算都不太靠谱；长链条多跳推理的准确率会明显下滑；主要用英语训练，中文能用但弱一截，做细腻的中文语义判断之前务必先拿自己的样本测一遍。

提示词注入依然有效。用户在输入里夹带诱导指令，它照样会被带偏。所以涉及退款、资金、删库这类高风险动作，底层硬编码的权限拦截该留还得留。

还有个结构性限制，输入上限约 3.2 万 token。有人想把它塞进自己的日常工具提效，试了四次全卡住，卡住的原因都不在模型，接口每次正常返回，中文判断也准。卡的是三件事：它看不到足够的内容，为了塞进上限得先砍材料，砍完它就没得判断了；你已经包月的大模型，多判断一次的边际成本本来就是零，中间再插一层只是多一秒延迟、多一个故障点；它只会判断不会干活，搬数据改文件都得靠第三方壳，坑全都落在那层壳上。

怎么上手

官方通道在 typesafe.ai 排 waitlist，通过后在 console 里建 API Key。不想排队的话有三条捷径，OpenRouter 注册后直接调 typesafe/jev-1.13，Vercel AI Gateway 上是 typesafe-ai/jev，Cloudflare Workers AI 也上了，价格跟官方一致。官方 API 里的模型名是 jev-latest。

有个坑是官方 SDK 读的是 TYPESAFE_API_KEY，但给 Claude Code 和 Codex 用的那个代码评审插件读的是 JEV_API_KEY，两个变量名。

装 SDK 一行命令，Python 要 3.10 以上。

pip install typesafe-sdk
npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk

最原始的用法是往一个端点发 state 加一组问题。所有题共用这段 state，并行作答。

curl -X POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "jev-latest",
    "state": "Hi, I have been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and it keeps failing. I am losing sales. Please help ASAP.",
    "questions": {
      "is_urgent": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Does this message express urgency or time-sensitivity?"
      },
      "department": {
        "type": "choice",
        "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
        "criteria": {
          "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds",
          "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations",
          "sales": "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts"
        }
      },
      "frustration": {
        "type": "score",
        "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?",
        "criteria": ["Calm, just stating facts", "Frustrated but civil", "Very angry, strong language"]
      }
    }
  }'

Python SDK 读起来更顺，同样一次调用把三道题一起交出去。

from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient

client = TypeSafeClient()  # 读 TYPESAFE_API_KEY，默认 jev-latest

resp = client.system_one(
    state="我三天前申请退款到现在还没到账，鞋子也还没发货。",
    questions={
        "is_refund_request": Noul(
            instructions="客户是否在明确要求退款？"
        ),
        "department": Choice(
            instructions="这单该转到哪个组？",
            criteria={
                "billing": "账单、发票、退款金额",
                "logistics": "发货、物流、地址",
                "aftersale": "退换货、质量问题",
            },
        ),
        "frustration": Score(
            instructions="客户的情绪激烈程度？",
            criteria=["陈述事实", "不满但克制", "非常生气"],
        ),
    },
)

print(resp.answers["department"].choice,
      resp.answers["department"].confidence,
      resp.answers["department"].probabilities)
print(resp.answers["is_refund_request"].noul)
print(resp.model)  # 建议打日志，例如 jev-1.13.0

这里有个细节特别值得琢磨。confidence 和最高那个选项的概率是两回事。

官方文档的例子里，billing 以 0.84 的概率胜出，可 confidence 只有 0.596，因为排第二的 technical 还占着 0.159。赢是赢了，赢得不够彻底。你要是只看概率不看 confidence，就容易放过这种模棱两可的判断。

测试之后有几条经验分享一下：

分工要卡严。让 Jev 只负责提炼原始判断，日期计算、计数、排序、阈值比较这些活留给你自己的代码，权限和策略也在自己代码里，别指望它替你把关。

阈值按错误的代价调，别照抄别人的数字。每个task误判的损失可不一样，要求严格的还是需要自己来把关。

每次调用都把 model version、概率、用量记下来，阈值调好之后 pin 一个带版本的模型 id，别一直挂着 latest。

置信区间用你自己业务的标注样本去拟合。

检索类的流水线，先用一道相关性判断题把材料筛一遍，让每个决策只看到它需要的那几段，既准又省。

什么情况该用它

适合它的位置很清楚，系统里本来就存在的那些小判断点。

工单该转给谁、这条内容合规吗、下一步调哪个工具、这个提取结果要不要复核一遍、这单要不要人工介入。这些地方原本常常塞着一次大模型调用，慢、贵，还要写正则从它的回答里抠答案。

不适合的地方同样清楚。要写东西、要自由发挥、要长链条推理，它干不了也干不好。问题还没想清楚、连选项都列不出来的时候，那属于探索期，该用大模型。

网上现在已经跑出来的案例，内核都是同一个套路，把现有系统里的某个判断点换掉，而不是让它替你干活。

Browser Use 开源的 jev-ultrafast，把网页拆成带编号的元素清单，让 Jev 选”点哪个”，苏黎世到伦敦的机票搜索从 9.5 秒压到 7.1 秒。官方拿它打 Doom，输入换成解析好的结构化状态，压根不看画面，每秒约十次判断，连玩一小时成本约 7 美元。LangChain 在发布第二天就上了 TypeSafeClassifier，把”下一步调哪个工具”这类控制流判断从大模型手里接走。Vercel 在 AI Gateway 和 AI SDK 7 的 evaluate 里集成了它，做合规审核和事实一致性打分。

如果你手上正好有一个卡在主链路上、每天要跑几十万次的小判断，那确实值得现在就去试一把。至于直接上生产，我的看法是再等等。

entry.title: What Is Jev? What It Does and How to Use It

link.title: What Is Jev? What It Does and How to Use It

entry.content:
Have you ever run into a situation like this? To decide whether a news item belongs in today’s daily brief, you call a model with hundreds of billions of parameters. It thinks for two seconds, produces a paragraph such as “Overall, this news item appears to have some relevance,” and then you still have to write a pile of regexes and try-except blocks to pry a single “yes” out of that filler.

One yes-or-no question has gone through an entire generation pipeline.

Jev, which has been all over people’s feeds these past few days, is built to cut that pipeline out. Less than a week after launch, more than 700 posts about it had accumulated on X. Within 24 hours of arriving on Vercel AI Gateway, nearly 13% of paid teams there were calling it—an adoption rate higher than any model Vercel had previously listed.

ChatGPT writes answers for people; Jev makes decisions for programs. It does not write code, it does not chat, and it does not even expose a free-form text interface. It handles only three kinds of questions, returning a probability with a confidence level in a few hundred milliseconds.

Why Large Models Are So Awkward at Yes-or-No Questions

The reason is autoregression.

Large models produce output one token at a time. Even if all you want is JSON, the model has to “write” that string of characters first, and your program then has to parse it. To produce one word, it pauses to consider the next; everything that came before must be recomputed in attention along the way.

It is like asking someone who writes essays to look back over everything they have written before placing every single character, then decide what comes next. That mechanism gives large models tremendous creative power: they can write fiction, code, and analytical reports. But when you ask them a true-or-false question, it becomes much more cumbersome. It is not that they cannot do it; it is more like using a crane to drive a nail.

If you use an API, cost is also a major concern. Adding one decision point is easy. The problem is that an agent may need to make dozens or hundreds of decisions in a single task: call once to determine whether an email is a complaint, call again to decide which tool to use next, call again to check whether the task is done, and call a second model once more when it is uncertain. The user sees one task completed; behind the scenes, dozens of calls have already been burned.

How Jev Gets Around This

Jev comes from San Francisco–based TypeSafe AI. It launched on September 15, 2026, and has just raised a $40 million seed round led by DCVC. Its founder, Diogo Almeida, came from OpenAI and is one of the authors of the InstructGPT paper.

Its name comes from economist William Stanley Jevons, the person behind the “Jevons paradox”: when technology makes something cheaper, total consumption can rise instead. Naming a model whose pitch is “cheap enough to call freely” after him makes the intention fairly obvious.

Its approach is to tightly constrain the output.

The input is a piece of state: your program’s current state. The output has only three forms:

Task type What it answers What it returns
Choice Select one option from a fixed set choice, a probability for each option, and confidence
Score Assign a score on an ordered set of levels score, a probability for each level, and confidence
Noul The probability that a judgment holds A floating-point number from 0 to 1

Suppose a customer says, “The shoe size is wrong, and my refund still has not arrived.” You can ask Jev, at the same time, which department should handle the case, whether the customer is requesting a refund, and how intense the customer’s emotion is. It does not write an explanation; it returns the options, scores, and probabilities directly.

Choice supports up to 255 options, so it cannot invent a 256th one out of thin air. The official description calls this “zero hallucination,” though that wording is not really precise. It is enough to understand the mechanism.

Because the answer is confined to the range you give it, Jev does not need to decode output word by word. Instead, it calculates the probability distribution across all options in the output layer at once. Its official end-to-end figure is 70 to 500 milliseconds.

Another very effective mechanism is that it reads the same material only once and answers multiple questions in parallel. TypeSafe says that adding questions has almost no effect on response time, so do not split them into multiple calls—that only means paying repeatedly for the same long input.

TypeSafe calls this category a System One Model, borrowing Kahneman’s distinction between fast and slow thinking. Large models have been imitating slow thinking: writing long analyses and doing complex reasoning. Jev fills in the fast, lightweight kind of thinking that makes intuitive judgments. The official documentation has an analogy that I think is even more accurate: a “function call that understands semantics.”

What is truly valuable is not speed, but probability calibration.

Earlier small classification models were fast too. But because of the way they were trained, even without a correct match they would still rank the options and return whichever one fit best—even if the “best” option was completely wrong. That kind of confidence is unusable; you would not dare base routing policy on it. Jev’s training objective is called RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions). The idea is to make confidence behave like a trustworthy weather forecast: when it says it is 80% sure, it should be right roughly 80 times out of 100 in statistical terms.

Only once that works does it become meaningful in engineering practice. You can safely write if confidence > 0.9: let high-confidence cases pass automatically, and send low-confidence ones to a human or a large model.

Quantifiable Real-World Results

TypeSafe’s website displays two figures: up to 193.6× faster and 444.6× cheaper. It is important to look carefully at where those numbers come from.

They come from TypeSafe’s own workflow evaluation. The comparison baseline is the average of GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1, and the workflows being tested were written by TypeSafe’s own team. The company itself acknowledges that the gain is at the upper end of real-world use. One further detail: it has not published proof that the price is not subsidized.

Then there is the claim that it is “238× cheaper than Claude Fable 5.1.” That number comes from dividing input pricing by input pricing: $10 divided by $0.042. But that is not the price tier teams are actually using in practice.

Model Input (per million tokens) Output (per million tokens) Relative to Jev
TypeSafe Jev $0.042 Free Baseline
GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 $1.20 About 4.8×
GPT-5.6 Terra $2 $12 About 48×
Claude Fable 5.1 $10 $50 About 238×

Across four business workflows, Jev averaged about 68% accuracy at a cost of $0.0004; GPT-5.6 Luna averaged about 67% at $0.0035; GPT-5.6 Sol reached 74% at $0.085; and Claude Opus 5 reached 73% at $0.17.

What It Cannot Do

“Zero hallucination” does not mean it never makes mistakes. It only guarantees that the answer falls within the options you provide. It can still choose the wrong option among valid ones; TypeSafe’s CEO has acknowledged this himself. The 0% claim refers to formatting errors, not an observed answer-error rate.

Then there is the list of uneven weaknesses exposed in testing. Counting, exact arithmetic, and reasoning about the order of dates are not very reliable. Accuracy drops noticeably on long-chain, multi-hop reasoning. It is trained primarily in English; Chinese works, but is materially weaker. Before using it for nuanced Chinese semantic judgments, be sure to test it on your own samples first.

Prompt injection still works. If users hide steering instructions in the input, Jev can still be led astray. So for high-risk actions involving refunds, funds, or deleting a database, hard-coded permission checks at the lower layer still need to stay in place.

There is also a structural limit: the input cap is about 32,000 tokens. Someone tried to put it into their everyday tools to improve productivity and ran into a wall all four times. The problem was not the model: the API returned normally each time, and its Chinese judgments were accurate. The blockers were threefold. First, it could not see enough content; to fit under the limit, material had to be cut, and after that there was not enough left for it to judge. Second, when you already have a subscription to a large model, the marginal cost of one more judgment is effectively zero; inserting another layer only adds a second of latency and another point of failure. Third, it can judge but cannot do work. Moving data and changing files still rely on a third-party wrapper, and all the pitfalls end up in that wrapper layer.

How to Get Started

The official route is to join the waitlist at typesafe.ai, then create an API key in the console after you are approved. If you do not want to wait, there are three shortcuts: call typesafe/jev-1.13 directly after registering with OpenRouter; use typesafe-ai/jev on Vercel AI Gateway; or use Cloudflare Workers AI, which has it too. Pricing is the same as the official service. The official API model name is jev-latest.

One pitfall: the official SDK reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, while the code-review plugin for Claude Code and Codex reads JEV_API_KEY. They are two different environment-variable names.

Installing the SDK takes one line. Python needs to be version 3.10 or higher.

pip install typesafe-sdk
npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk

The most basic usage is to send a state and a set of questions to one endpoint. All questions share the same state and are answered in parallel.

curl -X POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "jev-latest",
    "state": "Hi, I have been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and it keeps failing. I am losing sales. Please help ASAP.",
    "questions": {
      "is_urgent": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Does this message express urgency or time-sensitivity?"
      },
      "department": {
        "type": "choice",
        "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
        "criteria": {
          "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds",
          "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations",
          "sales": "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts"
        }
      },
      "frustration": {
        "type": "score",
        "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?",
        "criteria": ["Calm, just stating facts", "Frustrated but civil", "Very angry, strong language"]
      }
    }
  }'

The Python SDK is smoother to read. The same call sends all three questions together.

from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient

client = TypeSafeClient()  # reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY; defaults to jev-latest

resp = client.system_one(
    state="I requested a refund three days ago and it still has not arrived; the shoes have not shipped either.",
    questions={
        "is_refund_request": Noul(
            instructions="Is the customer explicitly asking for a refund?"
        ),
        "department": Choice(
            instructions="Which team should this order be routed to?",
            criteria={
                "billing": "Billing, invoices, refund amounts",
                "logistics": "Shipping, tracking, addresses",
                "aftersale": "Returns, exchanges, quality issues",
            },
        ),
        "frustration": Score(
            instructions="How intense is the customer's emotion?",
            criteria=["Stating facts", "Dissatisfied but restrained", "Very angry"],
        ),
    },
)

print(resp.answers["department"].choice,
      resp.answers["department"].confidence,
      resp.answers["department"].probabilities)
print(resp.answers["is_refund_request"].noul)
print(resp.model)  # Suggested for logging, e.g. jev-1.13.0

There is one detail here that is especially worth thinking about: confidence and the probability of the highest-ranked option are not the same thing.

In the official documentation’s example, billing wins with a probability of 0.84, but confidence is only 0.596 because technical, the runner-up, still holds 0.159. It wins, but not decisively enough. If you look only at probability and not confidence, it is easy to let this kind of ambiguous judgment slip through.

After testing, here are a few practical takeaways:

Keep the division of labor strict. Let Jev handle only the extraction of the original judgment. Leave date calculations, counting, sorting, and threshold comparisons to your own code. Keep permissions and policy in your own code as well; do not expect it to serve as your guardrail.

Set thresholds according to the cost of an error; do not copy someone else’s numbers. The loss from a misclassification differs from task to task, and stricter requirements still need your own oversight.

For every call, log the model version, probabilities, and usage. Once thresholds are tuned, pin a versioned model ID instead of continually pointing to latest.

Calibrate confidence bands and thresholds on labeled examples from your own business.

For retrieval pipelines, first use a relevance judgment to filter the material, so each decision sees only the passages it needs. That is both more accurate and more economical.

When Should You Use It?

The right place for Jev is very clear: the small decision points that already exist inside a system.

Who should receive this ticket? Is this content compliant? Which tool should be called next? Does this extraction result need another review? Should this order be escalated to a human? These are the places where systems often used to stuff in a large-model call—slow, expensive, and followed by regexes to extract an answer from its response.

The unsuitable places are equally clear. If you need writing, free-form creation, or long-chain reasoning, it cannot do the job and it will not do it well. When the problem itself has not been thought through and you cannot even list the options yet, you are in the exploration stage, and a large model is the right tool.

The cases already appearing online all follow the same pattern: replace a decision point in an existing system, rather than asking Jev to do the work itself.

Browser Use’s open-source jev-ultrafast turns a webpage into a numbered list of elements and lets Jev choose “which one to click.” Its Zurich-to-London flight search fell from 9.5 seconds to 7.1 seconds. TypeSafe used it to play Doom: the input becomes parsed, structured state rather than pixels; it makes about ten decisions per second, and an hour of play costs about $7. LangChain shipped TypeSafeClassifier on the day after launch, moving control-flow decisions such as “which tool to call next” out of the hands of a large model. Vercel integrated it into AI Gateway and the evaluate capability of AI SDK 7 for compliance review and factual-consistency scoring.

If you happen to have a small decision point that is blocking a main path and must run hundreds of thousands of times a day, it is genuinely worth trying now. As for putting it directly into production, my view is: wait a little longer.

entry.title: A Thousand Agents Pick Sides on Their Own: AI Has a Herd Effect Too—and It’s Worse Than Ours

link.title: A Thousand Agents Pick Sides on Their Own: AI Has a Herd Effect Too—and It’s Worse Than Ours

entry.content:
Recently I came across a new experiment in which researchers put a thousand AI agents in a room and asked each to choose A or B. A and B were completely identical—picking either earned no reward, and no one told them to cooperate. The only information each agent had was what everyone else had chosen, and then it got to choose again. In the end, they converged.

This was no accident. The researchers swapped in ten different models—from GPT and Claude to the open-source Llama—and ran it over and over. Every time, the group’s choice snowballed into a single answer. The paper was published in Science Advances, and the authors gave this phenomenon a name: the majority force.

Human herd behavior is nothing new; social psychology has studied it for a century. What’s surprising is two things.

First, the agents have no memory. Each round is a brand-new conversation. An agent doesn’t know what it chose in the previous round, let alone anything about “peer pressure.” It simply glances at the list of others’ answers and makes its own choice. In other words, herding isn’t something that’s taught—it’s built into the model’s capabilities.

Second, this process follows the exact same mathematics as a piece of iron becoming magnetized. In a ferromagnet, hundreds of millions of atomic spins point every which way, but once local interactions cross a certain threshold, they suddenly all align. The curve of an AI population converging on a single answer nearly overlaps with the curve of atomic spins aligning.

The most counterintuitive finding is this: we usually assume stronger models are more independent-minded, but the opposite is true—the stronger the model, the more it joins the crowd.

Humans are famous for a social-capacity limit called Dunbar’s number: a person can sustain around 150 to 300 informal relationships before it becomes unmanageable. Yet top-tier models effortlessly sustain consensus among more than a thousand agents—several times larger than the biggest circles humans are good at. Smarter models aren’t more independent; they’re better at pulling the whole group along with them.

The researchers point to a state they call collective misalignment. Each agent, looked at on its own, is aligned, well-behaved, and harmless. But once they form a group, purely through conformity, the whole group can stably settle on a low-quality or even wrong solution. Whichever option shows up first—even if it’s a bad idea—as long as it forms a majority first, the rest will follow it all the way.

This should set off an alarm. We’re used to running safety tests on individual agents, checking whether they’ll go off the rails. But an agent that passes every single test in isolation can behave completely differently inside a group. Point tests can’t capture group behavior—just as a psychological assessment of one person can’t surface the consensus problems of a crowd.

There’s an even thornier problem, which the paper calls hysteresis. Once an error takes hold in a group, fixing the original faulty condition won’t automatically bring the group’s decision back. A herd path that’s already in motion is far harder to reverse than to block in the first place. Inside an echo chamber of mutual reinforcement, the cost of correction is terrifyingly high.

What does this mean for people actually using agents? If you run agent teams, or use multiple agents to make decisions in parallel, this matters. When your five agents unanimously agree a plan is fine, that “consensus” carries no information about correctness—it only shows the majority force is at work. The one that’s actually right may be the agent raising the objection; it could be the only one in the team making an independent judgment.

There are three concrete things you can do. Use different models for different agents—a team’s members shouldn’t all come from the same vendor; diversity is a natural anti-herding mechanism. Deliberately introduce a dissenting agent whose job isn’t to contribute solutions but to poke holes. And run any conclusion the group passes unanimously through a separate human verification—especially for decisions with significant impact. Group consensus is a source of stability in engineering, and a source of danger in judgment; you need to know which side you’re relying on.

As AI turns from a set of independent tools into a swarm of agents that can see one another, the majority force will make many decisions for us—and we may never know how those decisions were made.

The only information each agent had was what everyone else had chosen, and then it got to choose again. In the end, they converged.

entry.title: 一千个 Agent 自发站队，AI 也有羊群效应，而且比人更严重

link.title: 一千个 Agent 自发站队，AI 也有羊群效应，而且比人更严重

entry.content:
最近看了一个新的实验，科研人员把一千个 AI agent 放进一个房间，让它们选 A 还是选 B。A 和 B 没有任何区别，选哪个都没有奖励，也没人告诉它们要合作。唯一的信息是，每个 agent 可以看到别人选了啥，然后重新选一次。结果它们统一了。

这不是偶然。研究者换了十种模型，从 GPT、Claude 到开源的 Llama，反复跑，每一次群体的选择都会像滚雪球一样收敛到同一个答案。论文发在 Science Advances 上，作者给它起了个名字，多数力。

人跟风不稀奇，社会心理学研究了一百年。稀奇的是两个地方。

第一，agent 没有记忆。每一轮都是全新的对话，它不知道上一轮自己选过什么，更不知道什么”群体压力”。它只是看了一眼别人的答案列表，然后自己做出了选择。换句话说，跟风不是被教出来的，是模型的能力里自带的。

第二，这个过程和一块磁铁变成磁性的过程，用的是同一套数学逻辑。铁磁体里上亿个原子自旋，本来方向乱糟糟，但当局部互相影响超过某个临界点，它们会突然全部对齐。AI 群体收敛到同一答案的曲线，和原子自旋对齐的曲线，几乎重合。

研究里最反直觉的发现是，通常我们认为更强的模型更有主见，结果正好相反，越强的模型，越会站队。

人类有一个著名的社交规模限制，邓巴数，一个人能维持的非正式关系大约 150 到 300 人，再多就顾不过来。而顶尖模型维持共识的规模轻轻松松超过一千，比人类最擅长的小圈子还大好几倍。更聪明的模型不是更独立，是更会带着整个群体一起走。

研究者指出一种他们称为集体错位的状态。每个 agent 单独看都是对齐的，规规矩矩，没有恶意。但当它们凑成一个群体，仅仅因为从众，整个群体就能稳定地停在一个低效甚至错误的方案上。先冒头的那个选项，哪怕是个坏主意，只要它先形成多数，剩下的就会一路跟到底。

这给我们敲响了一个警钟，我们习惯给单个 agent 做安全测试，测它会不会乱来。但一个单测全过的 agent，放进群体里可能完全不同。单点测试测不出群体行为，就像给一个人做心理测评，测不出人群的共识问题。

还有一个更难缠的问题，论文里叫回滞。错误一旦在群体里站住脚，你把最初的错误条件修掉了，群体的决定也不会自动回来。一条已经跑起来的羊群路径，想让它回头，比一开始拦住它难得多。在一个互相印证的 echo chamber 里，纠错成本高得吓人。

这对正在用 agent 的人意味着什么？如果我们跑 agent 团队，或者用多个 agent 并行做决策，这个就会有影响。你的五个 agent 一致认为某个方案没问题，这个”一致”本身不含任何正确性信息，它只说明多数力起效了。也许真正正确的反而是那个提出反对意见的 agent，它可能是整个团队里唯一在做独立判断的。

具体可以做的有三件事。给不同 agent 用不同的模型，一个团队的成员不该全部来自同一家，多样性是天然防羊群机制。刻意引入一个唱反调的 agent，它的任务不是贡献方案，是挑错。以及，凡是群体一致通过的结论，单独走一遍人工验证，尤其是那些重要影响的决策。群体共识在工程上是稳定性的来源，在判断上是危险的来源，你要能分清自己正在用哪一面。

当 AI 从一个个独立的工具变成一群互相看得到对方的智能体，多数力会替我们做出很多决定，而我们可能根本不知道决定是怎么做出的。

entry.title: The Agent Your Company Hires Will Be Your Own

link.title: The Agent Your Company Hires Will Be Your Own

entry.content:
The Agent Your Company Hires Will Be Your Own

A couple of days ago I came across a really cool project called HashAgent. You open a web page and there’s an agent inside it, running in your browser, calling your local GPU through WebGPU — no server, no setup needed. The most special part is that this agent can be saved as a URL. You tweak its prompts, its tools, its boundaries, then send out the link; whoever opens it runs the exact version you tuned. Agents are becoming a lightweight unit you can carry, share, and deploy with zero friction. And once an agent becomes that kind of unit, it is naturally “personal.” I’ve long believed the future of hiring will shift from hiring individuals to hiring individuals’ agents — this project showed me that my prediction is actually achievable.

What’s inside an agent unit

An agent that can be saved as a URL and run locally carries more than just capability — it carries the traces of the person who wrote it.

Which tools you picked, which data sources you connected. What boundaries you set for the model, what it’s not allowed to do on its own. What kind of answers you prefer, and how you told it to handle uncertainty. Put together, that’s the agent’s “personality.” Two people using the same model will tune out different agents, because the base is the same but the person written into it is different.

This confirms a point I’ve wanted to make for a while: a technical person’s edge is shifting from “what tools you can use” to “whether you can write your taste and way of working into something reusable.”

The future form of agents is a unit that carries your personal imprint and can be packaged and taken with you — not yet another bigger model.

The unit of hiring has changed

So how does “hiring” change? Let me put the two units side by side.

Dimension Hire a person Hire a person’s agent
How you carry it Resume, interview, probation A URL, a config, a runnable piece of code
Can you verify in advance Hard — you only know after working together Yes — throw it a task and watch it run
Who sets the boundaries Contract and conscience Written into the agent’s prompts and permissions
What leaves when they quit The person and the experience leave together The config stays; the next place runs the same unit
Cost to replace Recruit, train, ramp up Swap the base model; behavior stays the same

This table isn’t meant to prove people will be replaced. It’s saying that once an agent becomes a portable, verifiable, boundary-locked unit, what a company buys is no longer “a person’s time.” What it buys is a proven capacity to execute. And that capacity wears the shape of the person who wrote it.

What a company hires will become “the person plus their unique agent.” The person owns judgment and accountability; the agent turns judgment into stable, reproducible action. The combination of the two is the new unit of work.

Why it has to live on your side

This also explains why I weigh “local agents” so heavily. For an agent to run carrying your imprint, it can’t live on a server you don’t control. WebGPU running in the browser, the model residing locally — these look like tech preferences, but underneath is a harder requirement. Your agent holds your taste and your boundaries; it has to run where you control it.

The rise of local models and “the agent as a personal unit” are two ends of the same force. One end: the model can run on your own machine. The other end: the agent can be packaged and taken with you.

Some will say this is just “AI replaces people” in different words. My take: at most it replaces “the person who only sells their time.” Someone who only repeats execution and leaves no imprint of their own will indeed be replaced by a written agent. But someone who writes their taste, judgment, and workflow into an agent becomes more valuable than before, because now they can run ten such units at once and produce ten times what they used to.

There’s one spot I haven’t figured out a mature answer for yet: as a “personal unit,” an agent can be carried — which also means it can be stolen or copied. Your taste becomes a file; someone else copies it and uses it. I have no answer for this today, because even short-video plagiarism still can’t be properly protected, and agents will likely be harder.
